title: What Should Morphology Instruction Look Like?
author: Timothy Shanahan
summary: A reader asks Shanahan for a grade-by-grade list of morphemes to teach in K-5, on the model of the Fry sight word list, and Shanahan answers that no such list exists and then turns the question over to two scholars of morphological instruction, Jeffrey and Peter Bowers. Peter Bowers argues that a scope and sequence of morphemes is the wrong unit of planning altogether. What matters instead is a scope of orthographic concepts, taught by starting from words children already know, analyzing them into bases and affixes with word sums, and gathering related words into a matrix. Bowers presses the case for Structured Word Inquiry as a more accurate account of how English spelling works than phonics alone, because English preserves the spelling of a morpheme even when its pronunciation shifts. Shanahan does not fully concede the point. He still sees value in moving from simple phonics toward morphology, and he defends the usefulness of the kind of list the teacher asked for, noting that published lists of common prefixes and suffixes already exist and can be folded into word sums and matrices. The piece closes on teacher knowledge, arguing that effective morphology instruction requires both pedagogical technique and content knowledge about the language that many teachers currently lack.
points: Shanahan concedes that no grade-leveled list of morphemes comparable to the Fry sight word list exists, and uses the gap to bring in two outside scholars.
Peter Bowers recommends teaching whole morphological families at once through word sums and matrices rather than working through a sequenced list of affixes.
The argument turns on a claim about English orthography: spelling stays consistent across a morpheme even when pronunciation changes, as in act and action.
Bowers presents Structured Word Inquiry not as morphology bolted onto phonics but as a fuller explanation of grapheme-phoneme correspondences.
Shanahan defends the practical value of affix lists and closes by arguing that teachers need content knowledge about language, not just pedagogical technique.
quotes: A morpheme is the "smallest grammatical unit." It isn't the same thing as a word, and yet many words are morphemes. The distinction turns on whether the unit (the morpheme or word) can stand on its own.

Instead of a "scope and sequence" of morphemes to teach, what I recommend is starting with words in the children's vocabulary, analyzing such words to find their bases, then looking for other members of that family.
English spelling prioritizes consistent spelling of morphemes over consistent pronunciation of morphemes.

this is why Structured Word Inquiry (SWI) is not about "adding" morphological instruction to phonics instruction — it's about teaching how the system works. This is why I argue that SWI teaches grapheme-phoneme correspondences more explicitly and accurately than phonics.
To determine that two words share a base, we need evidence from both structure (word sum) and meaning (etymology).
Many teachers, when referring to morphology or "structural analysis," are talking about affixes alone, and not the bases.

I don't disagree with Peter on this overall, though I see more benefit of starting with simple phonics and working towards morphology and I'm not quite as dismissive of the kind of list that this teacher requested

For instruction to be effective, teachers require two types of knowledge. They need to have the kinds of pedagogical knowledge described here, so that they will know how to engage their students with morphology in effective ways.
